chapter: 14.6 Optimizer & Schedule: Muon + MuonClip and Warmup-Stable-Decay
core_intuitions: Muon orthogonalizes the momentum update: the raw update is dominated by a few large singular directions (the network races along those and starves the rest); setting every singular value to 1 makes the update push equally hard in every direction — a cheap spectral preconditioner (~Shampoo) built from matmuls only.

The hybrid is mandatory, not a compromise: Muon only makes sense for 2D feature-mixing matrices (attention projections, SwiGLU); the tied embedding has sparse per-row gradients and 1D RMSNorm gains have no matrix structure, so both stay on AdamW for per-coordinate adaptive rates.

RMS-matching (multiply the orthogonal update by 0.2*sqrt(max(m,n))) is what lets ONE conceptual learning rate govern both optimizers; forget it and Muon's raw update (RMS ~ 1/sqrt(max(m,n))) is tiny, so the run looks dead.

QK-clip caps attention logits by rescaling W_Q and W_K each by sqrt(tau/S_max), exploiting the bilinearity of the logit; under GQA the shared W_K must be scaled ONCE per KV group by the group's worst logit, never once per query head, or a shared key read by several tripping heads gets over-shrunk.

WSD has a schedule-agnostic constant-LR plateau you can extend at will (no baked-in endpoint), then a 1-sqrt decay to ~0 whose characteristic sharp loss drop is exactly the mid-training window where you anneal on premium data — a hook cosine cannot cleanly provide.

new_figures.name: muon-orthogonalization-spectrum
new_figures.concept: Muon replaces the momentum update with its polar factor UV^T, flattening the singular-value spectrum to all-ones so the update pushes equally along every direction.
new_figures.rationale: This is THE mechanism of the chapter and the one idea readers most often hold only verbally ('orthogonalize the update'). Seeing a skewed spectrum collapse to a flat all-ones spectrum, paired with a stretched ellipse becoming a circle, converts the abstract 'set every singular value to 1' into a concrete geometric intuition of 'equal push in every direction' and 'stop starving the small directions.'
new_figures.placement: Why Muon, and Why a Hybrid (anchor after the paragraph explaining orthogonalization of the momentum update, ~line 11)
new_figures.brief: A two-panel side-by-side infographic titled 'What orthogonalization does to the momentum update.' LEFT panel, header 'Raw momentum buffer B': a bar chart of ~6 singular values sigma_1..sigma_6 that decays steeply — sigma_1 tall, the rest progressively tiny (a few directions dominate). Directly beneath it a small 2D geometric inset: a cloud of unit gradient directions mapped through B rendered as a long thin ELLIPSE stretched along one axis, captioned 'learns fast along the long axis, starves the rest.' RIGHT panel, header 'Orthogonalized UV^T': the SAME six singular values now all equal height, sitting on a dashed guide line marked '= 1' (flat spectrum). Beneath it the geometric inset is now a CIRCLE, captioned 'equal-magnitude push in every direction.' Between the two panels a bold right-arrow labeled 'Newton-Schulz x5 (matmuls only, bf16)'. A thin caption strip along the bottom: 'Adam rescales each coordinate independently and never sees the matrix; Muon flattens the whole spectrum — a cheap spectral preconditioner (~ Shampoo without the inverse).' Constraints: singular-value heights are illustrative only (relative bars, no numeric labels except the dashed '1' line); use one theme accent for the bars and a neutral fill for the ellipse/circle; keep both ellipse and circle fully inside their insets and everything inside the viewBox; clear left-to-right reading order. Must be fully legible in both light and dark themes (no hardcoded primary colors).

new_figures.name: wsd-schedule-anneal
new_figures.concept: The three phases of Warmup-Stable-Decay, why the stable plateau is extendable, and why the decay phase doubles as the premium-data annealing window — contrasted with cosine.
new_figures.rationale: WSD is inherently a curve, and its whole payoff (an extendable flat plateau + a late sharp loss drop aligned with a data-mix shift) is spatial/temporal and hard to hold from prose. One infographic that stacks the LR curve, the data-mix band, and the loss curve on a shared time axis makes the capstone's central 'decay phase IS mid-training annealing' claim click, and the dashed cosine overlay makes 'why not cosine' obvious at a glance.
new_figures.placement: The WSD Schedule: Warmup-Stable-Decay (anchor after the piecewise eta(t) definition, ~line 205)
new_figures.brief: A wide infographic sharing one horizontal training-step axis (0 -> T, with tick marks and labels T_w = warmup end, T_s = stable end, T = final step). THREE stacked, vertically-aligned lanes over the same x-axis. LANE 1 (learning rate eta(t)): a solid accent curve that ramps LINEARLY up from 0 during warmup, holds a FLAT plateau at eta_max through the long stable phase, then follows a 1-sqrt-shaped DECAY curving down to ~0 during the final phase. Overlay a DASHED muted comparison curve = cosine that begins decaying immediately after warmup and floors at a small nonzero level (~eta_max/10) — visibly never reaching zero — labeled 'cosine: baked-in endpoint, floors above 0.' Shade three faint vertical bands behind the curve: 'Warmup' (narrow), 'Stable' (wide, annotated with a small 'extend at will ->' arrow and the note 'no baked-in endpoint; branch decay runs from a stable checkpoint'), and 'Decay' (annotated '= mid-training annealing, Ch 14.8'). LANE 2 (data mix, a horizontal band the same width): during the stable band it reads 'bulk FineWeb-Edu'; across the decay band it visibly gradient-shifts to 'Cosmopedia / math / code (premium)'. LANE 3 (loss, small curve): a gentle downward drift through warmup+stable, then a characteristic SHARP DROP beginning right at T_s, annotated 'low LR + high-quality data = polish.' Constraints: axis labels are symbolic only (T_w, T_s, T, eta_max) — invent NO numbers; accent for WSD LR, muted dashed for cosine; band fills low-opacity so they read in both themes; keep all three lanes and their labels inside the viewBox with no overlap; reading order top (LR) to bottom (loss).

new_figures.name: qk-clip-gqa
new_figures.concept: GQA-aware QK-clip: scale each tripped query head's W_Q by sqrt(tau/S_max), but scale each SHARED W_K only once per KV group by the group's worst logit — avoiding multiplying a shared key repeatedly.
new_figures.rationale: The GQA subtlety is the one genuinely tricky, bug-prone detail of the MuonClip section ('a KV slice read by four tripping heads would be multiplied four times over'). A diagram of the 8->2 head mapping with the two distinct scaling loops makes the per-head vs per-group asymmetry visual and cements the bilinearity trick (sqrt on each factor).
new_figures.placement: MuonClip / QK-Clip: Taming Attention Logits (anchor after the GQA paragraph describing the two-loop fix, ~line 142)
new_figures.brief: A top-to-bottom diagram in three stacked parts. PART A (the bilinear cap): a compact box 'logit s ∝ W_Q · W_K^T / sqrt(d_h)', with the rule 'if S_max > tau: scale W_Q and W_K EACH by sqrt(tau/S_max)  =>  logit x (tau/S_max)  =>  lands at tau.' Include a tiny gauge/needle graphic: a needle pushed past a marked 'tau' line, then a curved arrow pulling it back exactly to tau. PART B (the GQA mapping, the centerpiece): a row of 8 small query-head squares Q0..Q7 above a row of 2 wider KV-head blocks K0, K1, with connector lines showing the 4:1 grouping (Q0-Q3 -> K0, Q4-Q7 -> K1; label 'group = n_heads/n_kv_heads = 4'). Highlight two query heads, say Q1 and Q2, as 'tripped (S_max > tau)'. Show TWO labeled scaling loops: Loop A 'per query head' — an arrow onto each tripped Qh applying its OWN sqrt(tau/S_h) to that W_Q slice; Loop B 'per shared KV head, ONCE' — a single arrow onto K0 applying sqrt(tau / S_group_max) where S_group_max is the worst logit among Q0..Q3, with a crossed-out ghost '(NOT x4)' beside K0 to depict the over-shrink trap that is avoided. PART C (caption strip): 'The head that set the group max lands exactly at tau; its groupmates get their shared key pulled slightly below tau — conservative and safe. QK-norm already bounds most logits; QK-clip is the rare backstop.' Constraints: small integers only (8 query heads, 2 KV heads, group 4); use a theme-safe highlight (not a hardcoded red) for tripped heads and the tau line; keep all squares, connectors, and labels inside the viewBox with an unambiguous top-to-bottom reading order.

new_figures.name: muon-rms-matching
new_figures.concept: Why a single learning rate governs both optimizers: the 0.2*sqrt(max(m,n)) scale lifts Muon's tiny raw update RMS up into AdamW's ballpark.
new_figures.rationale: The chapter flags forgetting this scale as 'the single most common way to get a bad Muon run' (dedicated warning box + a key takeaway). The intuition is a scale comparison and lands instantly as bars on a shared RMS axis, defusing the 'Muon looks dead' failure mode that pure prose leaves fuzzy.
new_figures.placement: The full Muon step and RMS matching (anchor after the paragraph deriving the 0.2*sqrt(max(m,n)) scale, ~line 84)
new_figures.brief: A compact horizontal bar comparison of per-element UPDATE RMS on a single shared axis (use a log-ish or clearly-broken scale so tiny and order-1 values coexist legibly). Three stacked bars, top to bottom: (1) 'Muon raw (UV^T)' — a very short bar labeled 'RMS ~ 1/sqrt(max(m,n)) — tiny for a 1408x512 matrix; at a normal LR the weights barely move ('dead').' (2) A transform arrow labeled 'x 0.2*sqrt(max(m,n))' lifting bar (1) up to bar (3). (3) 'Muon scaled' — a bar at 'RMS ~ 0.2', drawn immediately beside a fourth reference bar 'AdamW step: RMS ~ 1 (per-coordinate)', with a brace spanning bars 3 and 4 labeled 'same ballpark => one conceptual LR governs both (Muon ~0.02, AdamW ~3e-3).' Include a small side annotation deriving the RMS: 'a semi-orthogonal m x n matrix has min(m,n) unit singular values => Frobenius norm sqrt(min) spread over m*n entries => RMS = 1/sqrt(max).' Footer note in a muted tone: 'Forget the scale and the run looks stalled — check this first.' Constraints: RMS values are illustrative magnitudes only (0.2 and 1 are the ratio that matters; the 'tiny' bar is symbolic, not a claimed measurement); theme-safe accent for the Muon bars and a neutral tone for the AdamW reference; keep all four bars, the arrow, and the derivation note inside the viewBox with no overlap.

summary: This applied capstone chapter has NO existing figures and is dense with distinct, bug-prone mechanisms, so it is figure-poor / concept-rich and warrants a small set of foundational statics. I propose four, all static (a single frame conveys each core idea, so no long-animation is justified). Two priority-1 flagships carry the chapter: (a) muon-orthogonalization-spectrum, showing a skewed singular-value spectrum collapsing to all-ones with a stretched ellipse becoming a circle — the geometric heart of 'push equally in every direction'; and (b) wsd-schedule-anneal, a three-lane time-axis infographic (LR curve with cosine overlay, data-mix band, loss curve) that makes 'the decay phase IS the premium-data annealing window' and 'the plateau is extendable' obvious at a glance. A priority-2 qk-clip-gqa diagram nails the trickiest detail — the per-query-head vs once-per-KV-group scaling asymmetry under GQA. A priority-3 muon-rms-matching bar comparison defuses the chapter's most-emphasized failure mode ('Muon looks dead' without the 0.2*sqrt(max) scale). All briefs use symbolic/illustrative quantities only, are theme-safe, and fit inside the viewBox.
